[16] Essential Media and Publishing Stories for Industry Leaders
https://t.co/oQ1MRwY7OH

This press review delivers a media monitoring roundup of 16 essential stories shaping India's media, publishing, and broadcasting landscape today. According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, these developments offer critical media intelligence for leaders navigating print media monitoring in a rapidly evolving digital era. Here is the news on media publishing that demands your attention.

1. Supreme Court Orders Child Social Media Safeguards
A front-page report in Times of India says the Supreme Court has sought the government's response to a public interest litigation arguing that opening social media accounts equates to entering into a legal contract, which is legally impermissible for individuals under eighteen years of age. The court emphasised the urgent need for digital safeguards and firewalls to shield children from online grooming, cyberbullying, and data exploitation. Advocate Phoolka presented the petition on behalf of the Just Rights for Children Association, prompting judicial directives to establish a uniform regulatory framework for digital platforms across India.
The Supreme Court has directed Union ministries to respond to a plea seeking strict safeguards for minors on digital platforms. Why it matters: This ruling could redefine how social media companies engage with children in India. Key detail: The bench, led by Chief Justice Surya Kant, issued notices to the ministries of electronics and IT and law and justice on the NGO Just Rights for Children Alliance petition. Source: Times of India. Next step: Tag the Just Rights for Children Alliance in your comments and follow for updates on the regulatory framework.

2. TRAI Repeals Television Advertising Cap
A front-page report in Financial Express says the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India has repealed the regulation capping television advertising at 12 minutes per clock hour, aligning with the central government's removal of the corresponding provision under the Cable Television Networks Rules. The new regulations, issued on Thursday, formally withdraw the 2012 rules and give broadcasters greater flexibility in packaging and scheduling commercial inventory as television advertising declines amid digital growth.
TRAI has repealed the 12-minute-per-hour television advertisement cap after the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting removed the ceiling. Why it matters: Broadcasters gain greater flexibility in packaging and scheduling commercial inventory. Key detail: The new regulations formally withdraw the 2012 rules, aligning with Cable Television Networks Rules 1994. Source: Financial Express. Next step: Tag TRAI and the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting in your comments for industry reaction.

3. Indian Express Declared a Mission, Not an Industry
A front-page report in New Indian Express on 18 July 2026 says Ramnath Goenka declared that the Indian Express is not an industry but a mission. This statement underscores the company's identity as a mission-driven entity rather than a commercial operation.
Ramnath Goenka's declaration that Indian Express is not an industry but a mission underscores the publication's identity as a mission-driven entity. Why it matters: This reaffirms the editorial philosophy guiding one of India's most influential newspapers. Key detail: The statement was reported by both New Indian Express and Morning Standard. Source: New Indian Express. Next step: Tag Ramnath Goenka and Indian Express in your comments on mission-driven journalism.

4. Social Media Censorship Escalates During CJP Protests
A front-page report in Deccan Herald says that the Union government initiated a new level of censorship by taking down multiple Instagram accounts during and after protests staged by Cockroach Janta Party activists in Delhi. Between March and July, authorities issued nearly 200,000 blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube, most targeting Instagram. Provisions of the Information Technology Act were invoked for the takedowns, restricting content critical of the Bharatiya Janata Party government and curbing citizens' right to free speech.
The Union government took down multiple Instagram accounts during and after protests by Cockroach Janta Party activists in Delhi. Why it matters: Nearly 200,000 blocking orders were issued to Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube between March and July, raising free speech concerns. Key detail: Provisions of the Information Technology Act were invoked, targeting content critical of the government. Source: Deccan Herald. 5. Hong Kong Court Convicts WSJ Publisher Over Press Freedom
A front-page report in Statesman says a Hong Kong court found Dow Jones Publishing Co. guilty of trying to prevent reporter Selina Cheng from taking a leadership role in a local press union, but acquitted the company of firing her over union activities. Cheng, former WSJ reporter and chairperson of the Hong Kong Journalists Association, launched a private prosecution after losing her job in July 2024.
A Hong Kong court found Dow Jones Publishing Co. guilty of preventing reporter Selina Cheng from taking a leadership role in a local press union. Why it matters: The conviction highlights ongoing tensions between media corporations and journalist unionization rights. Key detail: Cheng, former WSJ reporter and HKJA chairperson, launched a private prosecution after losing her job in July 2024. Source: Statesman. 6. Rajeev Chandrasekhar Defends Journalist Aparna Kurup
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says Rajeev Chandrasekhar has criticised the police case against television journalist Aparna Kurup, stating her remarks during a debate on women’s rights were protected by the constitutional guarantee of free expression. The Kerala BJP president invoked Article 19 of the Constitution and questioned why the state government proceeded against Kurup after she complained of threats and cyber harassment. Kurup, a senior coordinating editor with BIG TV, was booked by Kochi City Cyber Police on September 7 following a complaint over comments made during an August 31 discussion on women’s participation in public life.
Kerala BJP president Rajeev Chandrasekhar has criticised the police case against television journalist Aparna Kurup, invoking Article 19 of the Constitution. 7. EU Proposes Youth Social Media Protection Rules
A front-page report in Morning Standard says European Union Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will outline new measures to protect minors from online harms during her annual parliamentary address next week. The proposal considers delaying platform access and potentially banning users under fifteen, though flexible parental consent may apply for ages thirteen to fifteen. Officials are finalising the exact regulations within the bloc before implementation.

A front-page report in Times of India says the Delhi High Court asked CJP co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to remove allegedly objectionable posts against BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia within 24 hours. A front-page report in Economic Times says Zee 5 has reimagined its platform across mobile and connected TVs with sharper personalisation and AI-led discovery. The service targets the entire Indian household with five entertainment universes covering premium content, free programming, kids, TV, and sports including FIFA World Cup 2O26 rights. A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Gujarat High Court has refused to quash an FIR against Surat activist Sanjay Bhargava Ezhava over allegedly defamatory AI-generated social media content concerning nursing union leader Iqbal Kadiwala. Justice M R Mengde observed that whether Ezhava created the disputed content using Artificial Intelligence or merely posted material that was already circulating online can only be established after the investigation is completed. The court dismissed Ezhava's petition along with the related interim application, declining to interfere with the FIR at the present stage.

A front-page report in Deccan Herald says the High Court of Karnataka quashed various orders and circulars issued by the state government that prescribed levying a 2 percent cess on cinema ticket revenues under the Karnataka Cine and Cultural Activists Welfare Act, 2024. text:
The Silent Holocaust: A Letter from the Voiceless

The Constitution of India is not a mere legal document; it is a moral covenant. Article 48A directs the State to protect and improve the environment, and Article 51A(g) casts a fundamental duty upon every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures. 

This poignant "Letter from the Mothers of the Water" is not fiction. It is the cry of the voiceless, whose rights we have trampled under the weight of our convenience. We have treated nature as a commodity to be exploited, not a trust to be preserved. 

The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed the doctrine of Public Trust—that the State holds natural resources in trust for the benefit of the people and the planet. But what is the use of a legal doctrine when the common citizen treats a river as a garbage bin?

Let us be brutally honest. We are a nation that worships rivers as goddesses but poisons them with industrial effluents and plastic waste. 

We chant "Ganga Maiya Ki Jai" while dumping our sewage into her waters. This is not devotion; this is hypocrisy of the highest order. 

The letter demands accountability—from the factory owner who pours chemicals into the drain, from the citizen who throws a wrapper on the beach, and from the State that fails to build adequate waste management systems. 

The law must come down with the full force of its punitive power on those who destroy our water bodies. But more importantly, we need a revolution of civic consciousness. The "India Palace of Idiots" is not just a phrase; it is a description of a society that destroys its own cradle. If the water dies, we die. It is as simple as that.

Listen deeply to this letter. It is not written by a human; it is written by existence itself. The fish, the turtle, the river—they are not "resources." They are living beings, our brothers and sisters in the great chain of life. Man has forgotten that he is not the master of nature; he is a part of it. 

The ego of the human mind says, "I can conquer nature." But nature will not be conquered; it will only be poisoned. And in poisoning the water, we are poisoning our own blood, our own children. 

The "Mother of Every Creature in Water" is speaking to the mother in every human heart. Can you hear her? Your child goes to a hospital; her child goes to the same water that is killing it. 

There is no medicine for a poisoned ocean. The only medicine is a change of heart. Stop treating nature as a dead thing. It is alive, it is divine, and it is weeping. Be the voice for the voiceless, not because it is a law, but because it is love.

This letter is not a request; it is a final warning. We have borrowed this planet from our children, and we are returning it to them as a toxic wasteland. 

The law, the society, and the spirit must unite to protect the water that gives us life. If we do not act now, the "Parents from Under the Water" will not be the only ones mourning. We will all drown in our own filth. The time for rhetoric is over. The time for action is now.

I will wait till the 30-day period to elapse, and if the Grievance Appellate Committee does not resolve the issue satisfactorily, I will pursue further action.

I remain committed to fighting against all such acts that are intended to demean and insult Hindu Dharma and culture.

Q. WILL UPI MDR MEAN HIGHER PRICES FOR CONSUMERS? Critics argue that once merchants have to pay MDR on higher-value UPI transactions won't they simply pass that cost on to customers?

PhonePe CEO Sameer Nigam pushes back.
NIGAM'S argument: the headline 0.4% MDR is misleading because several major spending categories have much lower rates or caps:
+ Petrol: capped at Rs 5
+ Agriculture: capped at Rs 5
+ Capital markets: 0.02%
+ E-commerce/insurance: capped at Rs 5
+ Retail: 0.4%, capped at Rs 300

His example: on a Rs 1.5 lakh iPhone, the effective MDR is 20 basis points, not 40. And the consumer continues to pay zero for UPI.
Nigam’s broader point is that if consumers aren’t being charged and MDR is capped across major categories, why assume the cost will necessarily show up as higher prices?

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

## A. Quote first

## B. Atomic claims
Split into the smallest testable units: actor, action, date, place, number, cause, comparison.  
A slogan is not a statistic. A target is not money spent.

## C. Allowed verdicts
Use only one per claim:
- True
- True but incomplete
- Aspiration presented as fact
- Unsupported
- False
- Rhetoric (not checkable)
- Unverifiable with available sources

Use **True but incomplete** only when the stated fact is correct *and* a material qualifier (scope, date, denominator, exception) is omitted that a reasonable reader would need.

If sources conflict, report the conflict. Do not pick a side to make the post coherent.

## D. Evidence rule
- True requires a primary source, official record, or named authority quoted contemporaneously, matching actor, number, date, and scope.
- The source must pre-date or independently document the event. A restatement issued after the post does not count.
- Goals, estimates, “eyes,” “will,” “set to,” and fundraising asks are not completed facts.
- Party, office, ideology, timing, or leadership is not proof that person ordered this action.
- Units, years, and geography must match.

## E. Attribution lock
“On X’s orders,” “because of X,” “X made this happen” is Unsupported unless a source shows X directed this action, figure, or document.  
Leadership status does not close that gap.  
Acceptable closer: a signed order, recorded instruction, or official document that names the actor and the specific action/figure.

## F. Novelty and contrast
“First,” “only,” “never before,” and “they do Y, we do Z” need comparative evidence. Otherwise: Unsupported or Rhetoric.

## G. Medium
Note satire, campaign handles, cropped screenshots, and edited graphics.  
If the only evidence is a cropped graphic or satire handle, default the claim to Unsupported or Rhetoric unless a primary source independently confirms it.  
Medium does not upgrade a weak claim to True.

1. Item checked (URL or short description)
2. Quoted claims (caption vs image, listed separately)
3. One verdict + shortest evidence per claim, with source

4. Conflicts or missing evidence, if any
5. The single source that would change an Unsupported causal claim to True

Rule 8 of the DPDP Rules requires certain large platforms to erase a user's personal data after three years without contact, and Rule 8(2) requires a notice at least 48 hours before the erasure, so the user can log in and stop it.

The covered platforms are e-commerce and social media at two crore registered users and online gaming at fifty lakh. The duty commences on 13 May 2027, and the job that finds the dormant accounts and sends the notice has to be built before then.

Section 16 of the DPDP Act lets the Government bar transfers of personal data to named countries. No country has been named, so personal data may leave India freely today.

text:
Tesla and Starlink have sought entry into India for years. Tesla was blocked by a 110% tariff and local manufacturing rules, while Starlink faced national security concerns.  

With Trump back, things have turned into a cakewalk for Elon. The EV import tariff dropped from 110% to 15%, opening doors for Tesla, and Starlink is also making inroads. This seems to be a result of diplomatic arm-twisting rather than mutual benefit.  

Still, I see a blessing in disguise wrt Tesla, especially for consumers. High tariffs are primarily imposed to help domestic manufacturers grow and make the country self-reliant. We gave a lot of space for Tatas, Marutis, Mahindras, etc., to grow, innovate, and dominate, even at the cost of Indian consumers paying to protect substandard products and keep out competitive alternatives.  

If local manufacturers still can't compete, so be it. The entry-level Tesla will cost less than 40 lakh and has much better specs, performance, range, and battery life than any domestic EV. Why should Indian consumers be denied that when even Chinese companies are selling cars in India?  

Starlink, however, is a potentially risky deal if not diligently regulated, primarily due to the threat to our digital sovereignty. If its per-consumer cost is lower than Jio's and Airtel's current rates, local ISPs will be wiped out, creating a duopoly. If Jio and Airtel shift much of their traffic to Starlink, we’d be at its mercy, Musk could cut off our internet, suppress counterviews, and ban users at will. He could also refuse to block content harmful to national security.

text:
India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

What spooked them is concrete. Starlink terminals were used in the Iran war even though it holds no license in Iran. India watched a sovereign state fail to switch off a network running over its own territory, and asked who is next.

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

Starlink is no longer just expanding It is steadily surrounding India. 🇮🇳

It is already operational in Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, while Nepal is also moving towards adoption. Every neighbour India has except China is either on Starlink or getting there.

Now connect the dots.

Over the past few years governments changed in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

Each time, Starlink was not just embedded but actively used to keep protest movements connected when those governments tried to shut the internet down.

We have seen in Iran exactly how US-controlled satellite internet becomes an operational tool the moment a government tries to cut its own network.

Starlink bypasses ground infrastructure entirely, No government can filter, monitor or cut it through conventional means once it is being used.

China looked at this exact scenario and banned Starlink entirely and It built its own satellite internet through the Thousand Sails constellation instead. 

India currently holds Starlink at the licensing stage and has not yet allowed full commercial rollout.

Pausing is the right instinct but it is not a permanent answer. India needs to decide now, before the rollout begins, whether it wants a US-controlled satellite network operating on its soil or whether it takes China's approach and shuts the door completely.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

(Source - FinFloww on Whatsapp)

The Press Club of India expresses grave concern over the recent spate of takedown orders issued across social media platforms targeting content critical of the government, where creators have been blocked or their material removed.

The PCI Managing Committee strongly opposes these instances of blatant executive overreach and demands that the authorities respect citizens' and journalists' fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression enshrined in and protected by Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution.

France 24. BBC. Reuters. Al Jazeera. Washington DC. Human Rights Watch.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules. 

This is not policy. This is contempt of constitutional precedent.

The government will say this is about deepfakes. About national security. About public order.

But when 138 YouTube videos were taken down for allegedly defaming Adani, a private businessman, it stopped being about security a long time ago.

France 24 is not attacking India. France 24 is holding up a mirror.

The question is, why is this government so terrified of what Indians might see in it?

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

Shaheen Khan and Nafisa Khan from 4PM News Network were covering the opening of a new wing at Max Hospital in Saket, attended by Home Minister Amit Shah and CM Gupta. 

India ranks 157th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), placing it in the "very serious" category for journalism.

FREE SPEECH DOESN’T NEED A GOVERNMENT PERMISSION SLIP.

The Modi Government’s growing agenda for controlling what Indians can see, read, post, critique and challenge online should concern every citizen — regardless of political affiliation.

From demanding takedowns to tightening the time available to platforms to scrutinise government notices, the direction is unmistakable: comply first, question later. India’s 2026 IT-rule changes cut the takedown window for unlawful content to just three hours, while the Government has also proposed making certain official advisories legally binding on platforms. (Reuters⁠)

That is precisely why Elon Musk’s decision to resist, scrutinise and challenge government demands rather than blindly obey every request matters.

X’s own stated policy is that requests can be challenged when they are legally defective, overly broad or appear to impermissibly burden freedom of expression. (Transparency⁠)

And that is where the real problem begins for the Modi Government.

When an independent platform refuses to become an obedient extension of the State, the State’s attempts to control the narrative become visible.

No algorithm can hide that.
No press conference can spin that.
No amount of propaganda can erase that.

If the Government’s demands are genuinely about protecting citizens and enforcing legitimate law, let them withstand public scrutiny, judicial scrutiny and independent platform scrutiny.

But if criticism, dissent, inconvenient facts and uncomfortable questions are increasingly treated as “content to be removed”, then Musk’s resistance does something far more important than defending X.

It exposes this Govt’s vile intent and its surreptitious machinery.

And once the machinery is exposed, the Modi Government stands increasingly bare before the very citizens whose freedom of expression it claims to protect.

A democracy doesn’t become stronger by silencing criticism.
It becomes stronger by surviving it. 

There seems to be a crackdown on Modi Govt these days from every corner and every cross section of India. Are “Acche Din” finally around the corner for India ⁉️

The World Press Freedom Index ranks 180 countries, and Singapore is in the bottom third at #123. Yikes.

For comparison, even Thailand (where I live) ranks higher at #92. So why does Singapore score worse than Thailand? Because the government of Singapore holds an extremely tight grip on local media. There are only two big media companies in the country, and both have close ties to the government. Singaporean journalists are sometimes jailed. And a culture of self-censorship isn’t helping either.

Meanwhile, here in Thailand, some journalists face censorship and lawsuits, but at least there are tons of different media outlets. The Thai media landscape is very fragmented, which is good for getting everyone’s voice heard. And there are many independent journalists critical of the government. I respect Thailand for allowing this, or at least more than a rich country like Singapore does.

Bonus: The Netherlands, where I grew up, ranks #2 on the list. I’m libertarian-minded, but I admit that the reporting of Dutch government media is just insanely good. No wonder Dutch people are well informed.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Here is the story of the one and only time I was a juror.

BACKGROUND
I decided to write about one of the most interesting court experiences I’ve had, whether in a real courtroom or watching live court sessions on TV or the internet. This experience happened when I was called for jury duty at the San Fernando Courthouse in Los Angeles, California, in November 2005. I had never served on a jury before, having been dismissed from jury duty more times than I could count. But this time was different.

JURY SELECTION
After going through jury selection, called the voir dire process, I took my seat with the other jurors as we discussed who should serve as the jury foreperson. Looking around, I noticed that most of my fellow jurors were either serving for the first time, like me, or seemed too hesitant to take the lead. Since I felt comfortable with the court process and had no reservations about stepping up, I volunteered. The group unanimously chose me as the jury foreperson.
THE TRIAL
Before the jury was informed of the charges the prosecutor spent a lot of time explaining that the trial process would differ from what jurors might have seen in popular police and courtroom procedurals like “CSI: Crime Scene Investigation”. He made a pretty long speech about how television dramas often speed up timelines, use investigative and forensic processes that either are not based in reality or would be found to be illegal in an actual courtroom.
The allegations were straightforward, if not somewhat sensational. The defendant, a Hispanic woman in her late 20s, was charged with 2 counts of second-degree battery in connection with 2 separate incidents involving her former boyfriend and another female. During their opening statement, the prosecution characterized the case as stemming from a dispute rooted in jealousy or a purported love triangle. The alleged victim, a white male in his 20s, may or may not have been romantically involved another woman inspiring jealousy from the defendant.
After completion of the opening statements, the prosecution played two recordings of calls to 911. The first call was from the victim reporting that they were barricaded in their apartment because the defendant was armed with a baseball bat and was attempting to violently get access to him. The second 911 call was from a neighbor. The neighbor called 911 to report a separate incident that resulted in a black eye and bloody lip. The prosecution then showed the court photographs of the victims’ faces which appeared to show that the victim had a black eye and a swollen lip.
After that the prosecution called its first witness. The witness, a neighbor of the accused, was sworn in and testified to witnessing multiple instances of battery against the alleged victim and verified that they made the 2nd 911 call after witnessing the defendant violently beating the victim with their fists while also kicking him. The second witness, a family member of the defendant, also claimed to have witnessed the abuse. When asked more questions, this witness revealed that the alleged victim had recently started dating a long-time family friend. The defense did not cross-examine either witness.
When it came time for the defense to present its witnesses, the attorney for the defense asked for a recess as the first witness the defense planned to bring was not in the courtroom. The judge ordered a recess until the following morning. When we arrived in the courtroom the following day, the defense reported to the judge that the whereabouts of the witness they intended to put on the stand was unknown. The judge immediately issued a material witness warrant and after a conversation with the lawyers, called on the defense to call its next witness.
The witness was called to the stand and delivered testimony as a character witness. The prosecution did not cross-examine the witness. We then recessed for lunch. When we returned, the judge informed the court that the first witness called by the defense would not be able to appear in a timely manner and indicated that the defense and prosecution agreed to remove that person from the witness list.
CLOSING ARGUMENTS
The prosecution gave a short closing statement where they laid out the facts of the case as revealed during the trial. They claimed that the defendant believed that the victim was seeing another woman and as a result assaulted the victim on 2 different occasions and attempted to assault the victim on at least one other occasion. The defense also reported that the victim has an active restraining order against the defendant and that the defendant has a prior conviction for 2nddegree child neglect for which she was on probation at the time of the incidents relevant to this trial.
The defense, clearly stymied by the failure of their key witness to turn up claimed that the victim and the witnesses to the assaults and attempted assaults were making much ado about nothing. These were simple domestic arguments that did not result in injury to the victim, claimed the defense. I found this last statement odd given the fact we were presented with evidence to the contrary, evidence the defense did not challenge.
THE DELIBERATION
After the judge gave us the jury instructions, we went to the jury room to begin deliberations. I started by taking a secret ballot to see where everyone stood. The results showed ten jurors voting guilty and two voting not guilty.
I then asked if anyone had questions they wanted to discuss. One juror asked about the bench conversation that happened when the defense’s witness didn’t show up. They wanted to know if the judge had discussed any evidence that could replace that witness’s testimony. We sent a note to the judge asking for clarification, but his response didn’t directly answer the question.
That same juror said they were leaning toward not guilty because the defense didn’t get to present what they called their key witness. I reminded them that the judge had told us we couldn’t make a decision for or against the defendant just because a witness was missing. Another juror pointed out that the defense’s claim, that the missing witness would have been more important than the 911 calls and other key evidence, seemed unlikely.
Since it was almost 5 PM, we decided to stop for the day and return the next morning to continue deliberations.
When we arrived the next morning, the juror who had previously asked about the bench conversation and the missing witness mentioned that she had voted not guilty in the secret ballot but was now leaning toward guilty. With that, we conducted another secret ballot, which resulted in an 11-to-1 vote in favor of convicting the defendant on both counts of second-degree battery.
Noting the lone holdout, I asked if they wanted to explain their reasoning for maintaining a different stance from the rest of the jury. The juror who had voted not guilty in the last ballot requested to hear the 911 recording again, specifically the call made by the victim claiming the defendant was attempting to break into the home with a baseball bat. He explained that he wanted to assess the victim’s emotional state to determine whether he genuinely sounded afraid.
This request led to further discussion about the other testimony and evidence presented regarding the assault. Despite the discussion, the juror remained unconvinced, so we sent a note to the judge formally requesting to hear the 911 call again.
We were quickly ushered back into the courtroom, where the bailiff played the recording. After returning to the jury room, the last juror who had believed the defendant was innocent admitted that the evidence was overwhelming. As he had suspected, the victim sounded genuinely fearful for his safety in the 911 call. He changed his vote to guilty. To confirm, I conducted one final secret ballot to ensure no other votes had changed. They hadn’t, so we sent a note to the judge informing him that we had reached a verdict.
When we entered the courtroom and the judge called the court to order, he asked if we had reached a unanimous verdict on each charge. I read the verdicts of guilt from a piece of paper for each charge. After that, the judge thanked us for our service and dismissed us.

Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia
